episodes.212242: Multiple thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across central and southwest Virginia as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds within the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.
episodes.212252: A cold front dropped into the area after a prolonged period of humid conditions. A few bands/clusters of thunderstorms developed resulting in several damaging wind gusts and sporadic large hail.
episodes.212311: A broken line of storms developed in west-northwest flow, sinking southward across the area bringing a few damaging wind reports and some marine wind gusts.
episodes.212312: A broken line of storms developed in west-northwest flow, sinking southward across the area bringing a few damaging wind reports and some marine wind gusts.
episodes.212361: A severe thunderstorm dropped one inch diameter hail during the afternoon of May 28th.
episodes.212397: On May 28th, an upper low was over the Great Basin. A shortwave propagating around this low helped prime the atmosphere for thunderstorm development. A dry, well-mixed boundary layer was present over far southwest Idaho leading to a severe wind threat. Further north into the west central Idaho mountains, effective shear was to 30-40 knots. This increased the hail threat north, in addition to the wind.
episodes.212445: Isolated gale-force wind gusts occurred offshore the Lower Florida Keys as an outflow boundary produced by earlier thunderstorms over nearshore Gulf of America waters moved southward, crossing over the oceanside reef.
episodes.212585: An impressively moist airmass was in place with dew points well into the 60s across north-central Idaho during the afternoon, contributing to high instability. A vigorous shortwave trough pivoted northwestward through the northern Great Basin, providing strong forcing for ascent. This forcing, in conjunction with daytime heating and destabilization along the high terrain, initiated supercell thunderstorms that produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across the region.
episodes.212587: A highly unstable environment developed across western Montana, fueled by pooling moisture and steep lapse rates. Shortwave energy rotating around a broader upper-level trough provided the necessary lift for convective initiation which resulted in large hail. As storms moved into the Idaho Panhandle and interacted with the local terrain, they organized into two distinct quasi-linear convective systems, producing widespread severe wind gusts across Lincoln and Flathead Counties.
episodes.212589: Between May 28 and June 4, 2026, a very slow-moving upper-level low-pressure system  over Montana tapped into moisture from the Gulf of America, bringing heavy and widespread precipitation to western Montana. Prior to this event, several locations had already received significant moisture in May, leaving soils saturated and mountain runoff elevated. The combination of intense rainfall and ongoing snowmelt led to swollen rivers, and overwhelmed small streams, and flooded local irrigation canals. Intense thunderstorms brought heavy rain-rates in Sanders County resulting in mudslides.
episodes.212893: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||Soils were already saturated from previous rainfall, then an additional one to three inches of rain fell over the area. One strip of three to four inches fell over portions of Gilmer, Lewis, and Barbour counties. This excessive rainfall prompted minor flooding on portions of the Little Kanawha and West Fork Rivers as well as flooded roads in Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Jackson, Lewis, Mason, Roane, and Randolph Counties. Mud and rock slides also occurred in Harrison and Wirt Counties.  Strong to severe thunderstorms in the afternoon of the 27th produced wind damage that download trees and power lines in Boone, Harrison, Mason, Jackson, Lewis, Roane, and Upshur Counties.
episodes.212908: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid-day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||With soils already saturated from previous rainfall, the additional one to three inches of rain that fell over southeast Ohio prompted more flooded roads in Gallia and minor flooding on portions of Duck Creek, the Muskingum River and Little Muskingum River.
episodes.212910: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||With soils already saturated from previous rainfall, the additional one to three inches of rain that fell over northeast Kentucky prompted more flooded roads in Greenup and minor flooding on portions of Tygarts Creek.
episodes.213026: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.
episodes.213207: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across North and Central Texas on May 27 and 28, triggered by a slow-moving upper-level disturbance. Although the majority of these storms remained sub-severe, a few produced large hail. Additionally, the slow progression of the system led to heavy rainfall and flash flooding in some areas.
episodes.213309: Fairly typical early summer conditions were seen 5/27 with MLCAPE nearing 2000 J/kg in the afternoon with weak steering flow aloft. Scattered diurnal convection brought a couple instances of nuisance flooding in Lexington County.
episodes.213318: On the evening of May 27th into the morning of the 28th, plenty of atmospheric moisture and lift led to training thunderstorms across the northeastern combined Panhandles. Some flooding eventually occurred in northern Lipscomb County due to the heavy and repeated rainfall. Going into the 29th, moisture and lift continued to lead to thunderstorms, some of which became severe with hail up to golf ball size and wind gusts up to 75 to 80 mph. On the 29th, storms were mainly across the southern TX Panhandle.
episodes.213363: Training thunderstorms affected Cocke county during the overnight and pre-dawn hours on May 28th. The result was numerous reports of flooding across the county.
episodes.213383: In a warm southwest flow regime ahead of a weak cold front, a very moist air mass combined with moderate instability and improved shear resulted in a couple of organized lines of storms with damaging winds. One moved across the far northeastern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain, including Warren and Halifax counties, while the other affected Chatham, Moore, and Lee counties. There were numerous reports of downed trees and power lines in these areas.
episodes.213407: A stalled upper level low pressure system resided over the western CONUS during the early morning hours of May 28, with several spokes of upper level energy moving across the Plains. This, in conjunction with a secondary upper level trough over the Great Lakes region and a slow-moving surface low pushing from the Red River into southern Nebraska led to showers and thunderstorms developing within the deep, moist airmass. As a result, multiple rounds of moderate rainfall fell over the Missouri Ozarks between May 28 and May 29, leading to widespread 3 to 4 inch rainfall accumulations. This heavy rainfall led to flooding of several low water crossings and road closures.
episodes.213667: A closed low in the area brought two rounds of isolated strong to severe thunderstorms to the region. The main hazard with storms was severe wind gusts.
episodes.213674: Heavy downpours occurred across portions of northeast LA during the afternoon hours of May 28. These downpours lead to multiple roads to be flooded.
episodes.213778: During the late afternoon and evening hours on May 27th, a cluster of strong to severe storms produced up to quarter sized hail across portions of Clark and Jackson counties. Additionally, some instances of tree damage due to straight-line winds were noted in Adams County.
episodes.213800: Scattered storms along and south of a stationary front resulted in locally heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding across southeastern Virginia on May 27.
episodes.213801: Scattered severe storms moved across central and eastern Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 27. These storms produced damaging winds and isolated hail.
episodes.213835: Persistent mid and upper-level troughing to the west and warm advection along the northern edge of enhanced Gulf low-level flow maintained a moist and unstable environment across the region. This regime was conducive for waterspout development and a couple were spotted over Lake Pontchartrain.
episodes.213836: Persistent mid and upper-level troughing to the west and warm advection along the northern edge of an enhanced Gulf low-level flow maintained a moist and unstable environment across the region. By late morning and afternoon, convection formed a slow-evolving cluster across southern Mississippi, with repeated storms producing very heavy rainfall. Flash flooding developed in the Pascagoula and Moss Point areas.
episodes.213932: A weak upper level trough extended from the Middle Red River Valley into the Lower Mississippi Valley during the morning hours of May 28th. Given that a very moist and unstable air mass was in place across North Louisiana, large scale forcing aloft from this weak trough contributed to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across much of Northeast Louisiana from the mid-morning to the late afternoon hours. These storms were efficient rainfall producers, contributing to locally heavy rainfall that fell across the city of Monroe in Ouachita Parish. Rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches fell in a short period of time across the city, which contributed to multiple streets being flooded throughout the University of Louisiana-Monroe campus.
episodes.214067: A few thunderstorms produced a few reports large hail.
episodes.214123: Scattered storms in central Louisiana produced flooding Rapides Parish.
episodes.214257: A line of thunderstorms developed along a cold front over central WI and tracked south into south central WI. One storm became severe producing damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.214278: An approaching frontal boundary to the Natural State at the beginning of the episode would become a stationary boundary as the upper level flow pattern would begin as an approaching positively-tilted trough axis which would become an omega block and lock the mesoscale feature of the stationary boundary in position across Arkansas leading to a multiple day period of severe weather.
episodes.214417: Westerly sea breeze pre-dawn convection produced a strong marine wind gust over Tampa Bay.

Widespread high water affected the Flathead River basin. Anticipating heavy rainfall, operators at the Hungry Horse Dam opened the spillway gates at 1137MST on May 28 to manage reservoir capacity, causing significant downstream rises. On Friday morning, May 28, the City of Columbia Falls temporarily closed the back portion of River's Edge Park to the public due to early inundation. The Flathead River at Columbia Falls (CFMM8) crested at 13.78 feet with a discharge of 46,400 CFS on the evening of May 29, remaining above the minor flood stage of 13.0 feet. A subsequent NWS flood survey on June 1 at 1025MST documented high water completely surrounding private residential properties near the confluence of the South Fork and Middle Fork of the Flathead River. Floodwaters fully encircled a home 1 mile west of Hungry Horse, though the water had not yet breached the structural foundation or entered the living spaces at the time of the inspection.
Several roads were flooded in Winnsboro, including Fair Avenue, Power Street, Kinloch Street, and Lowry Street.

Numerous reports of trees downed or large branches snapped throughout the Boise metropolitan area. The two points were based on two reports that reasonably capture the south to north extent of damage, with timing estimated by radar. Reports of storm damage extend as far west as Caldwell and as far east as Boise. With the extent of damage, and measured gusts nearby, this damage was likely caused by winds of at least 60 mph. This damage was caused by the same outflow boundary associated with thunderstorms.
